title: Empty, and never used up
hookLine: the Tao is empty like a bowl yet never runs dry; it blunts sharp edges and unties knots (Tao Te Ching 4)

lines: A CHAIN IN ONE TIGHT KNOT.
cards: A necklace chain comes out of the drawer in one tight knot. The first move is to pull, and the knot gets smaller and harder, a little bead of metal you could never pick apart. The way out is the opposite of pulling.
Lay it flat on the table. Loosen the middle with the tip of a pin. Give the loops room.
Slowly the knot opens, not because anyone forced it, but because someone made space inside it. Chapter four of the Tao Te Ching is about that kind of space.

teach.b: First, empty like a bowl. The chapter compares the Tao to the emptiness of a vessel: you can use it and use it, and it never fills up and never runs dry. Strange arithmetic.
Full things run out, and a full bowl can't take anything else. It's the empty part that does the work.
Second, deep, and nobody's child. The chapter calls the Tao so deep it seems like the ancestor of everything. Then it ends with a shrug that's almost funny: it doesn't know whose child the Tao is.
It only says the Tao seems to come before even the Lord on High.

teach.h: BLUNT THE SHARP, UNTIE THE KNOT.
teach.b: Third, blunt the sharp, untie the knot. In Legge's words: "We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things." Sharp points: the cutting remark, the edge in a voice.
Complications: tangles like the chain. The same lines come back in chapter fifty-six, as if the old master wanted them heard twice.
Soften your brightness, the chapter goes on, and settle in with the dust of everyone else.
Not shining at people, not standing above the tangle, but getting down next to it, the way you'd lay a chain flat and give it room.

how: Some Taoist meditation teachers use chapter four's lines about blunting sharp points and untying tangles as a reminder to soften and settle before sitting.

games.q: a necklace chain comes out of the drawer in one tight knot. what opens it?
o: grab two ends and pull hard.
lay it flat and loosen the middle, giving the loops room.
cut it and buy a new one.
games.why: pulling makes the knot tighter. making room inside it is what opens it, the way chapter four says to unravel the complications of things.

practice: Bring to mind one tangle in your life right now, a misunderstanding, a messy email thread, a decision you've been tugging at for weeks, and for now, just stop pulling on it.
Breathe into the middle of it and ask which one small loop could loosen first, the way a pin loosens a chain. If you pray, you can bring the knot into prayer; if not, keep breathing space into it.

orig.note: Chinese, chōng: empty, hollow. The word chapter four uses for the Tao's emptiness.
